[[File:Marchenko-Pastur distribution.svg|thumb|upright=1.75|Plot of the Marchenko-Pastur distribution for various values of lambda]]
{{Probability distribution
 | name       = Marchenko-Pastur
 | type       = density
 | pdf_image  =
 | cdf_image  =
 | notation   = <math>X \sim \mathrm{MP}(\lambda,\sigma^{2})</math>
 | parameters = <math>\lambda>0</math> aspect ratio (<math>\lambda=m/n</math>);<br /><math>\sigma^{2}>0</math> scale (entry variance)
 | support    = <math>x \in [\lambda_{-},\lambda_{+}]</math>, with <math>\lambda_{\pm}=\sigma^{2}(1\pm\sqrt{\lambda})^{2}</math>;<br />plus an atom at <math>0</math> of mass <math>1-1/\lambda</math> when <math>\lambda>1</math>.
 | pdf        = <math>f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{(\lambda_{+}-x)(x-\lambda_{-})}}{2\pi\sigma^{2}\lambda\,x}</math> for <math>\lambda_{-}\le x\le \lambda_{+}</math>, and 0 otherwise.<br />For <math>\lambda>1</math> add a point mass <math>1-1/\lambda</math> at <math>0</math>.
 | cdf        = <math>F(x)=0</math> for <math>x<\lambda_{-}</math>;<br />
<math>\begin{align}F(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^{2}\lambda}\Big[
&\sqrt{(\lambda_{+}-x)(x-\lambda_{-})}
\\&               - \tfrac{\lambda_{-}+\lambda_{+}}{2}\arccos\!\Big(\frac{2x-\lambda_{-}-\lambda_{+}}{\lambda_{+}-\lambda_{-}}\Big)
\\&               + 2\sqrt{\lambda_{-}\lambda_{+}}\arctan\!\Big(\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{-}}{\lambda_{+}}}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{+}-x}{x-\lambda_{-}}}\Big)
\\&               + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\big(\lambda_{-}+\lambda_{+}-2\sqrt{\lambda_{-}\lambda_{+}}\big)\Big]
\end{align}
</math><br />for <math>\lambda_{-}\le x\le \lambda_{+}</math>;<br />
               <math>F(x)=1</math> for <math>x>\lambda_{+}</math>.<br />For <math>\lambda>1</math>, add a jump of size <math>1-1/\lambda</math> at <math>0</math>.
 | mean       = <math>\operatorname{E}[X]=\sigma^2</math>
 | median     =
 | mode       = <math>0</math> if <math>\lambda>1</math><br /><math>\sigma^{2}\frac{(1-\lambda)^{2}}{1+\lambda}</math> if <math>0< \lambda\le 1</math>
 | variance   = <math>\sigma^{4}\lambda</math>
 | skewness   = <math>\sqrt{\lambda}</math>
 | kurtosis   = <math>\lambda+2</math> (excess <math>\lambda-1</math>)
 | entropy    =
 | mgf        = <math>M_X(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^{2}\lambda}\int_{\lambda_{-}}^{\lambda_{+}} e^{t x}\,\frac{\sqrt{(\lambda_{+}-x)(x-\lambda_{-})}}{x}\,dx</math> (continuous part). For <math>\lambda>1</math>, add <math>1-1/\lambda</math> from the atom at <math>0</math>.<br />
Bessel form (let <math>\alpha=\sigma^2(1+\lambda)</math>, <math>\beta=2\sigma^2\sqrt{\lambda}</math>, <math>\rho=\min(\sqrt{\lambda},\,1/\sqrt{\lambda})</math>,
<math>S_\rho(z)=I_0(z)+2\sum_{n=1}^\infty(-\rho)^n I_n(z)</math>):<br />
<math>M_X(t)= e^{\alpha t}\!\left[\frac{1+\lambda}{2\lambda}\,I_0(\beta t)
               - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\,I_{1}(\beta t)
               - \frac{|1-\lambda|}{2\lambda}\,S_{\rho}(\beta t)\right]</math>, and if <math>\lambda>1</math> add <math>1-\tfrac{1}{\lambda}</math>.
}}
In the mathematical theory of [[Random matrix|random matrices]], the '''Marchenko–Pastur distribution''', or '''Marchenko–Pastur law''', describes the [[asymptotic]] behavior of [[singular value]]s of large rectangular [[random matrix|random matrices]].  The theorem is named after [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] [[Ukrainians|Ukrainian]] mathematicians [[Volodymyr Marchenko]] and [[Leonid Pastur]] who proved this result in 1967.

If <math>X</math> denotes an <math>m\times n</math> random matrix whose entries are independent identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance  <math>\sigma^2 < \infty</math>, let

: <math>Y_n =  \frac{1}{n}X X^T </math>

and let <math>\lambda_1,\, \lambda_2, \,\dots,\, \lambda_m</math> be the [[eigenvalue]]s of <math>Y_n</math> (viewed as [[random variable]]s).  Finally, consider the random measure

: <math>\mu_m (A) = \frac{1}{m} \# \left\{ \lambda_j \in A \right\}, \quad A \subset \mathbb{R}, </math>

which is the empirical distribution, counting the number of eigenvalues in the subset <math>A</math> included in <math>\mathbb{R}</math>.

'''Theorem'''. {{Citation needed|date=January 2023|reason=Some discussion as to the veracity of the formula given}} Assume that <math>m,\,n \,\to\, \infty</math> so that the ratio <math>m/n \,\to\, \lambda \in (0, +\infty)</math>.  Then <math>\mu_{m} \,\to\, \mu</math> (in [[Weak_topology#Weak-*_topology|weak* topology]] in [[Convergence_in_distribution#Convergence_in_distribution|distribution]]), where
: <math>\mu(A) =\begin{cases} (1-\frac{1}{\lambda}) \mathbf{1}_{0\in A} + \nu(A),& \text{if } \lambda >1\\
\nu(A),& \text{if } 0\leq \lambda \leq 1,
\end{cases}
</math>
and
: <math>d\nu(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma^2 } \frac{\sqrt{(\lambda_{+} - x)(x - \lambda_{-})}}{\lambda x} \,\mathbf{1}_{x\in[\lambda_{-}, \lambda_{+}]}\, dx</math>
with
: <math> \lambda_{\pm} = \sigma^2(1 \pm \sqrt{\lambda})^2. </math>

The Marchenko–Pastur law also arises as the [[Poisson_distribution#Free_Poisson_distribution|free Poisson law]] in free probability theory, having rate <math>1/\lambda</math> and jump size <math>\lambda \sigma^2</math>.

== Singular value bounds in the large system limit ==

As the dimensions of a random matrix <math> \mathbf X  </math> grow larger, the max/min singular values converge to  <math> \|\mathbf X\|_F \left(\frac {1} {\sqrt{\min(m,n)}} \pm \frac 1 {\sqrt{\max(m,n)}} \right)</math>
.

These are useful ''approximations'' of singular value bounds for large matrices. For matrices of finite size as are typically encountered, they are more what you'd call "guidelines" than actual rules.

== Moments ==
For each <math>k \geq 1</math>, its <math>k</math>-th moment is{{sfnm|1a1=Bai|1a2=Silverstein|1y=2010|1loc=Section 3.1.1}}
:<math display="block">\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}\frac{\sigma^{2k}}{r+1}\binom{k}{r}\binom{k-1}{r} \lambda^{r} = \frac{\sigma^{2k}}{k}\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}\binom{k}{r}\binom{k}{r+1} \lambda^{r} </math>

==Some transforms of this law==

The [[Stieltjes transform]] is given by

: <math>s(z)=\frac{\sigma^2 (1-\lambda)-z - \sqrt{(z- \sigma^2(\lambda + 1))^2-4\lambda \sigma^4}}{2\lambda z \sigma^2}</math>
for complex numbers {{mvar|z}} of positive imaginary part, where the [[complex square root]] is also taken to have positive imaginary part.{{sfnm|1a1=Bai|1a2=Silverstein|1y=2010|1loc=Section 3.3.1}} It satisfies the quadratic equation
: <math>\lambda \sigma^2 z s(z)^2+\left(z-\sigma^2(1-\lambda)\right) s(z)+1=0.
</math>
The Stieltjes transform can be repackaged in the form of the R-transform, which is given by{{sfnm|1a1=Tulino|1a2=Verdú|1y=2004|1loc=Section 2.2}}

: <math>R(z)=\frac{\sigma^2}{1-\sigma^2 \lambda z}</math>

The S-transform is given by{{sfnm|1a1=Tulino|1a2=Verdú|1y=2004|1loc=Section 2.2}}

: <math>S(z)=\frac{1}{\sigma^2 (1 + \lambda z)}.</math>

For the case of <math>\sigma=1</math>, the <math>\eta</math>-transform {{sfnm|1a1=Tulino|1a2=Verdú|1y=2004|1loc=Section 2.2}} is given by <math>\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{1+\gamma X} </math> where <math> X </math> satisfies the Marchenko-Pastur law.

: <math> \eta(\gamma)= 1 - \frac{\mathcal{F}(\gamma,\lambda)}{4\gamma\lambda} </math>

where <math>\mathcal{F}(x,z)=\left(\sqrt{x(1+\sqrt{z})^2+1}-\sqrt{x(1-\sqrt{z})^2+1}\right)^2 </math>

For exact analysis of high dimensional regression in the proportional asymptotic regime, a convenient form is often <math>T(u):=\eta\left(\tfrac1u\right)</math> which simplifies to

: <math> T(u)= \frac{-1+\lambda-u+\sqrt{(1+u-\lambda)^2+4u\lambda}}{2\lambda}</math>

The following functions <math>B(u):=\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{u}{X+u}\right)^2</math> and <math>V(u):=\frac{X}{(X+u)^2}</math>, where <math>X</math> satisfies the Marchenko-Pastur law, show up in the limiting Bias and Variance respectively, of ridge regression and other regularized linear regression problems. One can show that <math>B(u)=T(u)-u\cdot T'(u)</math> and <math>V(u)= T'(u)</math>.

==Application to correlation matrices==
For the special case of correlation matrices, we know that 
<math>\sigma^2=1</math> and <math>\lambda=m/n</math>. This bounds the probability mass over the interval defined by 
: <math> \lambda_{\pm} = \left(1 \pm \sqrt{\frac m n}\right)^2. </math>

Since this distribution describes the spectrum of random matrices with mean 0, the eigenvalues of correlation matrices that fall inside of the aforementioned interval could be considered spurious or noise. For instance, obtaining a correlation matrix of 10 stock returns calculated over a 252 trading days period would render <math>\lambda_+=\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{10}{252}}\right)^2\approx 1.43</math>. Thus, out of 10 eigenvalues of said correlation matrix, only the values higher than 1.43 would be considered significantly different from random.
